options.D: The return on investment must be zero

q: A company retains its earnings instead of paying a dividend, yet a shareholder who needs cash income is, under the Modigliani-Miller reasoning, not worse off, because he can:

options.A: Sell a part of his shareholding in the market to realise the cash he needs, creating his own 'homemade dividend' while the value of his remaining holding reflects the retained earnings
options.B: Demand interest on the retained earnings from the company
options.C: Require the company to issue him debentures free of cost
options.D: Draw the amount from the company's cash credit account

q: A retired investor explains that he values a rupee of dividend in hand today more than a rupee of possible capital gain in a distant year, which he regards as far less certain. The dividend theory that rests on exactly this preference of investors is the:

options.A: Modigliani-Miller irrelevance theory
options.B: Residual theory of dividends
options.C: Pecking order theory
options.D: Bird-in-hand theory, associated with Gordon and Lintner

q: A company has earned good profits, but a loan agreement it signed earlier places a ceiling on the dividend it may pay until the loan is reduced. In deciding its dividend for the year, the binding consideration for the company is:

options.A: The dividend paid by a neighbouring company
options.B: The contractual restriction in the loan agreement, which limits the dividend regardless of the size of the profits earned
options.C: The market price of its share on the day of the meeting
options.D: The dividend it paid ten years earlier

q: Between two companies with the same average level of earnings, the one whose earnings are steady and predictable year after year can safely follow a higher dividend payout than the other. This is because:

options.A: Steady earnings are taxed at a lower rate
options.B: The law fixes a higher dividend for such a company
options.C: A stable inflow of earnings gives reasonable assurance that the dividend can be maintained in future years without strain, whereas widely fluctuating earnings call for a cautious, lower payout
options.D: Fluctuating earnings cannot be computed at all

q: The directors of a company propose to make up a shortfall in profits by paying the dividend out of the paid-up share capital of the company. This proposal is impermissible because:

options.A: A dividend may be paid only out of the profits of the company (current or accumulated, after providing for depreciation), and not out of its capital, which must be kept intact for the protection of creditors
options.B: A dividend may be paid only in the month of March
options.C: A dividend must always equal the whole of the profits
options.D: Share capital cannot appear in the balance sheet of a company

q: The earnings per share of a company are Rs 9 and it then makes a bonus issue of one share for every share held (1 : 1). Other things remaining the same, the earnings per share recomputed on the enlarged share capital are:
A company capitalises Rs 20,00,000 of its general reserve by issuing bonus shares. The immediate effect of this issue on the company is that:

options.A: Its total net worth (shareholders' funds) increases by Rs 20,00,000
options.B: Its reserves fall and its paid-up share capital rises by the same amount, the total net worth and the proportionate interest of each shareholder remaining unchanged
options.C: Its cash balance increases by Rs 20,00,000
options.D: Each shareholder's proportionate holding in the company doubles

q: A company splits each of its shares of Rs 50 into five shares of Rs 10 each. The effect of this split is that:

options.A: The paid-up share capital of the company increases five times
options.B: Fresh funds of four times the capital flow into the company
options.C: The number of shares increases five times and the face value per share falls to one-fifth, the total paid-up capital, reserves and each shareholder's proportionate interest remaining unchanged
options.D: The reserves of the company are converted into share capital

q: The profit after tax of a company is Rs 24,00,000 and the total dividend declared by it is Rs 9,60,000. Its retention ratio is:

options.A: 40 per cent
options.B: 36 per cent
options.C: 50 per cent
options.D: 60 per cent

q: An enterprise has earnings before interest and tax of Rs 12,00,000, pays interest of Rs 3,00,000 and a preference dividend of Rs 1,50,000, and the tax rate is 25 per cent. Its fixed charge coverage ratio, reckoning the preference dividend on a pre-tax basis, is:

options.A: 2.40 times
options.B: 4.00 times
options.C: 3.00 times
options.D: 1.80 times

q: A company wishes to reward its shareholders but is short of cash because its funds are committed to an expansion programme. A course that rewards shareholders while conserving its cash is to:

options.A: Pay a larger cash dividend by borrowing for the purpose
options.B: Declare a stock dividend (bonus shares) out of its reserves, giving shareholders additional shares without any outflow of cash
options.C: Sell a part of its plant to raise cash for the dividend
options.D: Postpone the wages of its staff to save cash for the dividend
